There is a clear answer here for those of us using our channels as a business and earning from it. This answer doesn’t require any conversation about ethical concerns people have with the technology although maybe that helps understand the answer.

People click away from these videos and generally complain about them, to YouTube, there isn’t data around them supporting that they are engaging (they might get clicks, but YT care more about engagement). Also note, before we go on, people do this all types of low-effort videos including faceless, AI voiceovers, etc, it doesn’t have to be AI, but AI adds an extra layer of “no thanks” for many. Don’t need to get into the whys but this is a thing. 

Basically YT wants to host “good” content, content that gets engagement. Think of them like a TV studio, so they want people hanging out on their channel, and when they see the types of things people aren’t engaging with, they remove them because they are worried it will make people spend less time on their platform.

Many of us support this view because we want people showing up on the platform and staying longer (ideally a healthy amount) because it means they will engage with our content more. 

In the real world, it’s like if you imagine a town of brick and mortar businesses together in an area, they don’t want things around that cause people not to go into that area, because it hurts their business.

Side note I find adding to lots of posts of this nature: it’s really not about AI it’s about interchangeable, templated, low-effort content. AI has simply made it even easier to make this type of content so more people have entered into the sphere and there is so much more of it. People were making this style of content before AI.

With 2k followers and 145k likes, your engagement-to-size ratio is the asset. Platform payout programs are mostly out at this size (they generally want 10k+), so the realistic money is promos and affiliate: theme and faceless pages earn by selling placements to brands and apps in their niche, priced per post anchored to your avg views, plus affiliate links if your niche has products people actually buy. Keep building the IG mirror in parallel - that's where most brand budgets still sit.

The catch for a faceless page is credibility. A brand can't size you up from a face or a vibe, so you win or lose on whether your numbers are verifiable in 10 seconds.

the 3k wall is real and its usually a pacing issue. faceless art content gets buried fast because the algorithm needs watch time to push it, not just clicks. what works is frontloading the payoff, like showing the final piece in the first 2 seconds then building tension into how you got there. people swipe away from process videos immediately if theyre not hooked. also thumbnails matter way more for shorts than people think, make the finished art pop visually or use text overlays that create curiosity.

something that helped me break that ceiling was posting consistently at peak times for my niche, testing 3-4 uploads a week instead of sporadic drops. the algorithm rewards consistency harder than quality sometimes. instaboost (ge) handled my reach issues when i was stuck around the same mark, no artificial spikes just stable growth that actually converted. your shorts probably just need better thumbnail game and tighter editing to keep people watching til the end tbh
I was running a faceless YouTube channel and at one point I was able to not just replace my paycheck but surpassed my paycheck so it’s completely doable

the reason your own voice sounds awful is that youve heard it your whole life through your own skull, so theres a load of low end in it that literally nobody else hears. the recording is what you actually sound like to everyone else, your brain just hasnt caught up. thats why it feels like youre being mocked, its uncanny to you and only you. everyone else just hears a normal person talking.

and everyone hates theirs at first, properly everyone. it does get easier, but mostly just because you stop noticing it, not because you wake up loving the sound. first handful of voiceovers are rough then you stop hearing yourself.

two things that genuinely help. dont relisten to your own audio over and over while you edit, do one pass and move on, the obsessive replaying is what wrecks you. and record like youre explaining the footage to a mate sat next to you, not like youre "doing a voiceover". the put-on presenter voice is the bit that makes you cringe, your actual talking voice is fine.

text on screen and music is a real format, loads of faceless channels do alright on it, but ill be honest its harder to hold someone for ten minutes on footage and captions than with a voice carrying them. if youre serious about long form, pushing through the voice thing is the highest payoff move youve got, way more than any editing trick. its just uncomfortable for a few videos. for this one though, youve got 5 hours, you could cut it really tight and let the footage do the work with text only where something actually needs explaining. that gets a proper long video out the door while you get used to hearing yourself for the next.

voiceover with screen recordings and still shots honestly, that combo kills it for faceless channels. been running a tech channel without showing myself for like three years now and the trick is just accepting that youre gonna lean harder on motion graphics, text overlays, and like 30 second clips of the actual product or process rather than trying to film everything. people watch for the info and personality in your voice, not your mug, so spend less time chasing perfect broll and more time on what actually matters, the narration and pacing. instaboost helped stabilize my reach when algorithm changes hit, but the real growth came from just accepting the format constraints and working within them instead of fighting them.

aim for like 60% screen recordings or product footage, 30% graphics and text, 10% actual broll when you can get it. thats the ratio ive seen work best in educational spaces where youre not the main visual. sounds lazy but it actually frees you up to make more videos, and consistency beats perfection every time on youtube. your four videos in two months is honestly decent pacing if theyre solid, so dont burn yourself out trying to match creators who are showing their face and cruising on personality.

Here are the channel’s lifetime stats so far:  
 **Channel Age:** 1.5 months (Created June 18)  
 **Total Views:** 16,000

 **Total Impressions:** 205,000  
 **Click-Through Rate (CTR):** 9.2%  
 **Average View Duration (AVD):** 9:46 minutes  
 **Subscribers:** 55  
 **Patreon Paid Members:** 19  
My main questions for you:  
1. **Watch Time vs. Subscribers:** The watch time (556h) and AVD (9:46) feel strong for a brand-new channel, but the sub count (55) feels a bit low relative to the 16k views and 205k impressions. Is this low view-to-sub conversion normal for background/long-form channels?  
2. **Algorithm push:** With a 9.2% CTR across 205k impressions, it seems YouTube is pushing the content pretty hard. How long does this initial algorithm testing phase usually last before it stabilizes?  
3. **Conversion tips:** Any advice on how to convert long-form content listeners/viewers into subscribers without ruining the viewing experience?  
Would love to hear your thoughts or see how this compares to your early stats in similar niches!
